Pattern 10 of 21

Binary Tree Traversal

Visit every node of a tree exactly once, in an order you choose on purpose. The order you pick (pre, in, post, or level) decides what information is ready when you reach each node.

1. What is this pattern for?

Imagine touring a company org chart. A preorder tour greets the manager first, then each team. A postorder tour collects every team's report first, then hands the summary to the manager. An inorder tour (in a sorted chart) meets people left to right, like reading names off a shelf. A level-order tour visits floor by floor: the CEO, then all VPs, then all directors.

A binary tree is a set of nodes where each node has a value and up to two children, left and right. Almost every tree problem is "walk the tree and do something at each node". The only real decision is when you do the work relative to the children:

OrderVisit sequenceUse it when the node needs…
Preordernode → left → right…to pass something down (depth, path so far, bounds). Also copying / serializing.
Inorderleft → node → right…sorted order in a BST (binary search tree).
Postorderleft → right → node…answers from its children first (height, sums, "best path below me").
Level orderrow by row, using a queue…anything per level: averages, right-side view, zig-zag, min depth.

The first three are depth-first: they go deep before going wide. You can write them with recursion (the computer's call stack remembers where you were) or with your own explicit stack. Level order is breadth-first and uses a queue.

2. How it works (bisected)

  1. Base case: empty tree. If node is None, there's nothing to do. Every recursive tree function starts here.
  2. Each node is touched three times. Recursion arrives at a node (1st touch), comes back after finishing the left subtree (2nd touch), and comes back after the right subtree (3rd touch). Preorder records on touch 1, inorder on touch 2, postorder on touch 3. That's the whole difference.
  3. Iterative = simulate the call stack. Push nodes you still need to return to. For inorder: slide left pushing every node, pop one, record it, then move to its right child.
  4. Level order = queue + frozen size. Put the root in a queue. While it's not empty, read size = len(queue); pop exactly size nodes (that's one level) and push their children for the next level.
  5. Pick the order from the question. Information flows down? Preorder. Up? Postorder. Sorted BST? Inorder. Per row? Level order.

3. Seeing a problem: how to spot tree traversal

Trigger words

  • "binary tree", "root", "TreeNode", "BST", "subtree", "ancestor", "leaf"
  • "each level", "level by level", "right side view", "zig-zag", "minimum depth" → level order
  • "kth smallest", "sorted", "validate BST", "successor" → inorder
  • "height", "diameter", "max path sum", "is balanced", "subtree sum" → postorder
  • "serialize", "clone", "construct from…", "path from root" → preorder

Shape of the input

  • A root: TreeNode, or a level-order list like [3,9,20,null,null,15,7].
  • The answer for a node depends on its subtrees (combine) or its ancestors (pass down).
  • Brute-force smell: you call a helper like height(node) from inside another recursion, re-walking subtrees over and over. That's O(n²). One postorder pass that returns the height while computing the answer is O(n).
The one question to ask"At this node, do I need information from above (pass it down: preorder), from below (return it up: postorder), in sorted order (inorder), or grouped by depth (level order)?"

4. When to use it, and when not to

Use tree traversal when…Prefer something else when…
The input is a rooted tree with left/right pointersNodes can have many neighbours and cycles: that's a general graph, use DFS or BFS with a visited set
You need per-level answers (level order)You need shortest distance in an unweighted graph or grid: use BFS (same queue idea, plus visited)
BST questions about order (inorder) or searching (walk one branch)You only need to find one value in a BST: just walk down one path, O(h), similar in spirit to Modified Binary Search
Subtree answers combine into parent answers (postorder)Overlapping sub-problems on sequences/grids: use Dynamic Programming (tree DP is postorder + memo)
You must explore all root-to-leaf pathsYou must build/undo choices to enumerate combinations: use Backtracking

Cost: every traversal is O(n) time (each node visited once). Space is O(h) for DFS (recursion/stack depth; h = log n if balanced, n if it's a stick) and O(w) for level order, where w is the widest level (up to n/2).

5. The Python templates (memorize these)

Each template below is written out in full, one small step per line. Read the code, then the plain-English walk-through underneath it. All of them use LeetCode's TreeNode (fields val, left, right).

A) Recursive DFS: one skeleton, three orders

# A) Recursive DFS skeleton: move ONE line to switch between pre / in / post
def dfs(node):
    # Base case: an empty subtree has nothing to visit, so stop here.
    if node is None:
        return
    # visit(node)  <- PREORDER  (work before children: pass info down)
    dfs(node.left)
    # visit(node)  <- INORDER   (work between: sorted order in a BST)
    dfs(node.right)
    # visit(node)  <- POSTORDER (work after: combine children's answers)

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. if node is None: return is the base case. Every recursive tree function starts with it; without it you would crash on None.left.
  2. dfs(node.left) then dfs(node.right) visit the two subtrees, left before right.
  3. The three # visit(node) comments mark the three moments a node is "touched": before the children (preorder), between them (inorder), after them (postorder). Put your real work on exactly one of those lines.
# A2) The three recursive orders, each one collecting values into a list.
# The recursion lives in a separate top-level helper ("..._walk").
# The helper receives the list "out" and adds values to it.

def preorder_walk(node, out):
    if node is None:              # empty subtree: nothing to add
        return
    out.append(node.val)          # PRE: record the node BEFORE its children
    preorder_walk(node.left, out)
    preorder_walk(node.right, out)


def preorder_rec(root):
    out = []                      # will hold the values in visiting order
    preorder_walk(root, out)      # the helper fills the list
    return out


def inorder_walk(node, out):
    if node is None:
        return
    inorder_walk(node.left, out)
    out.append(node.val)          # IN: record the node BETWEEN its children
    inorder_walk(node.right, out)


def inorder_rec(root):
    out = []
    inorder_walk(root, out)
    return out


def postorder_walk(node, out):
    if node is None:
        return
    postorder_walk(node.left, out)
    postorder_walk(node.right, out)
    out.append(node.val)          # POST: record the node AFTER its children


def postorder_rec(root):
    out = []
    postorder_walk(root, out)
    return out

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Each order has two functions: a small public one (preorder_rec) that creates the empty list out, and a recursive helper (preorder_walk) that fills it.
  2. The helper takes out as a parameter, so every recursive call appends to the same list. No nested functions are needed.
  3. The three helpers are identical except for where the line out.append(node.val) sits: first (pre), middle (in) or last (post).

Dry run on the tree [4,2,6,1,3,5,7] (4 at the root, 2 and 6 below it, then 1, 3, 5, 7):

FunctionResult
preorder_rec[4, 2, 1, 3, 6, 5, 7]
inorder_rec[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] (sorted, because it's a BST)
postorder_rec[1, 3, 2, 5, 7, 6, 4]

B) Postorder that returns a value

# B) Postorder that RETURNS a value up (height, sums, best path...)
def height(node):
    # An empty subtree has height 0.
    if node is None:
        return 0
    # First ask both children for their heights (children before parent = postorder).
    left_height = height(node.left)
    right_height = height(node.right)
    # This node adds one level on top of its taller child.
    taller_child = max(left_height, right_height)
    return 1 + taller_child       # the parent gets back one number

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. An empty subtree has height 0. That stops the recursion at the leaves' missing children.
  2. Both children are asked for their height first. Because the node waits for its children, this is postorder.
  3. max(left_height, right_height) picks the taller child, and 1 + counts the node itself.
  4. The function returns the number to its caller, which is how information flows up the tree.

Dry run on [4,2,6,1,3,5,7]:

Nodeleft_heightright_heightreturns
1 (leaf)001
3 (leaf)001
2112
6 (same as 2)112
4 (root)223

C) Iterative inorder

# C) Iterative inorder (the one interviewers ask for)
def inorder_iter(root):
    out = []                      # the values, in inorder
    stack = []                    # ancestors we still have to come back to
    current = root                # the node we are about to explore
    # Keep going while there is a node to explore OR an ancestor waiting on the stack.
    while current is not None or len(stack) > 0:
        # 1) Slide down-left, pushing every node we pass on the way.
        while current is not None:
            stack.append(current)
            current = current.left
        # 2) The top of the stack is the leftmost node we have not visited yet.
        current = stack.pop()
        out.append(current.val)
        # 3) Now explore that node's right subtree.
        current = current.right
    return out

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. out collects the answer, stack remembers ancestors we must come back to, current is where we are.
  2. The outer while runs as long as there is either a node to explore or an ancestor waiting.
  3. Step 1, the inner while: walk left as far as possible, pushing each node. This is exactly what the recursive version does when it calls dfs(node.left) again and again.
  4. Step 2: pop. The popped node has no unvisited left side any more, so it is next in inorder. Record it.
  5. Step 3: move to its right child and repeat. If there is no right child, current is None and the next loop pops an ancestor.

Dry run on [4,2,6,1,3,5,7]:

2[4, 2]2[1, 2]
3[4, 3]3[1, 2, 3]
4[4]4[1, 2, 3, 4]
5[6, 5]5[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
6[6]6[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
7[7]7[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]

D) Iterative preorder and postorder

# D) Iterative preorder: stack, push RIGHT before LEFT
def preorder_iter(root):
    if root is None:              # empty tree: nothing to visit
        return []
    out = []
    stack = [root]                # start with only the root on the stack
    while len(stack) > 0:
        node = stack.pop()        # take the most recently pushed node
        out.append(node.val)      # PRE: record it straight away
        # Push RIGHT first, so that LEFT ends up on top and is popped first.
        if node.right is not None:
            stack.append(node.right)
        if node.left is not None:
            stack.append(node.left)
    return out


# Iterative postorder: collect "root, right, left", then read it backwards.
def postorder_iter(root):
    if root is None:
        return []
    mirrored = []                 # will hold root, right, left order
    stack = [root]
    while len(stack) > 0:
        node = stack.pop()
        mirrored.append(node.val)
        # Push LEFT first, so that RIGHT is popped first.
        if node.left is not None:
            stack.append(node.left)
        if node.right is not None:
            stack.append(node.right)
    # Read "mirrored" from the last item to the first: that gives left, right, root.
    out = []
    i = len(mirrored) - 1
    while i >= 0:
        out.append(mirrored[i])
        i = i - 1
    return out

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. preorder_iter: the stack starts with just the root. Each loop pops one node and records it immediately (that's "me first").
  2. A stack is last-in-first-out, so the right child is pushed before the left child. That way the left child is on top and gets handled first.
  3. postorder_iter runs the same loop but pushes left before right, which produces "root, right, left" in mirrored.
  4. The final while i >= 0 loop copies mirrored from the last item to the first. Reversed, "root, right, left" becomes "left, right, root", which is postorder.

Dry run of preorder_iter on [4,2,6,1,3,5,7]:

E) Level order (BFS on a tree)

# E) Level order (BFS on a tree)
from collections import deque


def level_order(root):
    if root is None:              # empty tree: no levels at all
        return []
    result = []                   # one inner list per level
    # deque is a "double-ended queue":
    #   queue.append(x)  adds x at the BACK of the line
    #   queue.popleft()  removes and returns the item at the FRONT
    queue = deque()
    queue.append(root)
    while len(queue) > 0:
        # Freeze the size: exactly this many nodes belong to the current level.
        level_size = len(queue)
        level = []
        for _ in range(level_size):     # "_" means: we don't need the counter
            node = queue.popleft()      # oldest node first
            level.append(node.val)
            # Children go to the BACK: they belong to the NEXT level.
            if node.left is not None:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right is not None:
                queue.append(node.right)
        result.append(level)
    return result

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. An empty tree has no levels, so return [] right away.
  2. The queue starts with only the root. append adds at the back and popleft takes from the front, so nodes come out in the order they went in.
  3. level_size = len(queue) is read before the inner loop. At that moment the queue holds exactly one full level.
  4. The inner loop pops exactly level_size nodes, records their values, and pushes their children to the back. Those children wait for the next round.
  5. After the inner loop, level is complete and is added to result.

Dry run on [4,2,6,1,3,5,7]:

RoundQueue at startlevel_sizelevelQueue after
1[4]1[4][2, 6]
2[2, 6]2[2, 6][1, 3, 5, 7]
3[1, 3, 5, 7]4[1, 3, 5, 7][]

6. How to remember it forever

Memory hook: "The name tells you where the root goes"Pre = root first, In = root in the middle, Post = root last. Left always comes before right. Level order is the odd one out: it uses a queue, not a stack.

Picture

Trace a pencil around the outside of the tree, starting left of the root. You pass each node on its left side (pre), under it (in), and on its right side (post). Record the node at the matching moment.

Chant

"Pre: me first. In: me between. Post: me last. Level: one row at a time."

Direction rule

"Down = pre, up = post." Passing values to children? Preorder with parameters. Children reporting to the parent? Postorder with return values.

7. LeetCode problems, solved step by step

Helper used below: class TreeNode: val, left, right (LeetCode's standard definition).

Medium 230. Kth Smallest Element in a BST BSTStack

Problem: Given the root of a binary search tree and an integer k, return the k-th smallest value (1-indexed).

Spot it: "BST" + "kth smallest" = sorted order is needed. Inorder traversal of a BST visits values in ascending order.

Key insight: Use the iterative inorder so you can stop early the moment you've visited k nodes. Cost is O(h + k), not O(n).

Approach:

  1. Start with current = root, an empty stack, and visited_count = 0.
  2. Slide left: push current and move to current.left until current is None.
  3. Pop the top node. It's the next-smallest value. Add 1 to visited_count.
  4. If visited_count == k, return this value (stop early).
  5. Otherwise set current = current.right and repeat from step 2.
class Solution:
    def kthSmallest(self, root: Optional[TreeNode], k: int) -> int:
        stack = []                # ancestors waiting to be visited
        current = root            # where we are in the tree
        visited_count = 0         # how many values we have visited so far (in sorted order)
        while current is not None or len(stack) > 0:
            # Go as far left as possible, remembering the path on the stack.
            while current is not None:
                stack.append(current)
                current = current.left
            # The top of the stack is the next smallest value.
            current = stack.pop()
            visited_count = visited_count + 1
            # Is this the k-th smallest? Then stop early; no need to see the rest.
            if visited_count == k:
                return current.val
            # Otherwise continue with this node's right subtree.
            current = current.right
        return -1                 # only reached if k is bigger than the number of nodes

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. stack, current and visited_count are set up. The count tells us how many values we have seen in sorted order.
  2. The inner while slides left from current, pushing every node. The smallest unvisited value ends up on top of the stack.
  3. stack.pop() gives the next smallest value, so visited_count goes up by 1.
  4. If the count has reached k, that value is the answer and we return immediately, without visiting the rest of the tree.
  5. Otherwise current = current.right: the next bigger values live in the right subtree (or in an ancestor on the stack).

Dry run on root = [5,3,6,2,4,null,null,1], k = 3:

StepStack after sliding leftPoppedvisited_countAction
1[5, 3, 2, 1]111 ≠ 3, go right (None)
2[5, 3, 2]222 ≠ 3, go right (None)
3[5, 3]33count == k, return 3

Complexity: O(h + k) time, O(h) space.

Medium 98. Validate Binary Search Tree BSTStack

Problem: Return True if the tree is a valid BST: every node's left subtree holds only smaller values, its right subtree only larger values, recursively.

Spot it: "valid BST" means "is the inorder sequence strictly increasing?"

Key insight: Checking only node.left.val < node.val is the classic trap. In [5,4,6,null,null,3,7] the 3 is a right-subtree descendant of 5, which breaks the rule, but every parent-child pair looks fine. Comparing each inorder value with the previous inorder value catches it.

Approach:

  1. Run the iterative inorder traversal (slide left, pop, go right).
  2. Keep previous_value = the last value you popped.
  3. Each time you pop a node, if previous_value exists and current.val <= previous_value, the order isn't strictly increasing: return False.
  4. Update previous_value and continue. If the traversal finishes, return True.
class Solution:
    def isValidBST(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> bool:
        stack = []                # ancestors waiting to be visited
        current = root
        previous_value = None     # the value we visited just before (None = nothing yet)
        while current is not None or len(stack) > 0:
            # Slide left, pushing every node.
            while current is not None:
                stack.append(current)
                current = current.left
            # Visit the next node in inorder.
            current = stack.pop()
            # Inorder of a BST must be STRICTLY increasing.
            if previous_value is not None:
                if current.val <= previous_value:
                    return False  # out of order (or a duplicate): not a valid BST
            previous_value = current.val
            # Move on to the right subtree.
            current = current.right
        return True               # every value was bigger than the one before it

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Same iterative inorder as before, plus previous_value, the last value we visited (None at the start).
  2. The inner while slides left, pushing nodes. stack.pop() then gives the next value in inorder.
  3. If there is a previous value and the current one is not bigger, the inorder sequence is not strictly increasing, so the tree is not a BST: return False.
  4. Otherwise remember this value in previous_value and go to the right subtree.
  5. If the loop finishes without a problem, every value was bigger than the one before it: return True.

Dry run on root = [5,1,4,null,null,3,6] (expected False):

StepStack after sliding leftPoppedprevious_valueCheck
1[5, 1]1Nonenothing to compare, OK
2[5]515 > 1, OK
3[4, 3]353 <= 5, return False

Alternative (preorder, passing info down): check(node, lo, hi) requires lo < node.val < hi, then recurses with (lo, node.val) on the left and (node.val, hi) on the right.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space.

Medium 105. Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal Binary TreeHash Map

Problem: You get the preorder and inorder lists of a tree with unique values. Rebuild the tree.

Spot it: "construct from traversals" means you have to know exactly what each order guarantees.

Key insight: Preorder's first value is always the root. Find that root in inorder: everything to its left is the left subtree, everything to its right is the right subtree. Keep a pointer into preorder and build left before right, because preorder is root → left → right. A hash map gives O(1) lookups of positions in inorder.

Approach:

  1. Build a map value → index in inorder for O(1) lookups.
  2. Keep a pointer self.next_root into preorder. The value there is the root of the subtree you're about to build.
  3. The helper method build(low, high) builds the subtree whose values are inorder[low..high]. If low > high, return None.
  4. Take preorder[self.next_root] as the root, advance self.next_root, and find its inorder position middle.
  5. Build the left subtree from (low, middle-1) FIRST, then the right subtree from (middle+1, high). That's the same order preorder uses.
class Solution:
    def buildTree(self, preorder: List[int], inorder: List[int]) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        # Remember where each value sits in "inorder", so we can find it in O(1).
        self.index_in_inorder = {}
        for i in range(len(inorder)):
            value = inorder[i]
            self.index_in_inorder[value] = i
        # Keep preorder on self so the helper method can read it.
        self.preorder = preorder
        # Position in preorder of the next root we will create.
        self.next_root = 0
        # Build the whole tree: it uses every position of inorder, 0 .. n-1.
        return self.build(0, len(inorder) - 1)

    def build(self, low: int, high: int) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        # Builds the subtree made of the values inorder[low..high] (helper method).
        if low > high:
            return None           # empty range: no subtree here
        # The next value in preorder is the root of this subtree.
        root_value = self.preorder[self.next_root]
        self.next_root = self.next_root + 1
        node = TreeNode(root_value)
        # Everything left of the root in inorder is its left subtree, the rest is its right.
        middle = self.index_in_inorder[root_value]
        node.left = self.build(low, middle - 1)      # LEFT first: same order as preorder
        node.right = self.build(middle + 1, high)
        return node

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The for loop builds self.index_in_inorder: value → its position in inorder. Looking up a root's position is then O(1).
  2. self.preorder and self.next_root are stored on self so the helper method build can read and advance them across recursive calls.
  3. build(low, high) builds the subtree whose values are inorder[low..high]. If the range is empty (low > high), there is no subtree: return None.
  4. The value at preorder[self.next_root] is the root of this subtree (preorder always lists the root first). We create the node and move the pointer forward.
  5. middle is where that root sits in inorder. Positions low..middle-1 are its left subtree, middle+1..high its right subtree.
  6. The left subtree is built before the right one, because preorder lists root, then all of the left subtree, then the right.

Dry run on preorder = [3,9,20,15,7], inorder = [9,3,15,20,7] (each row is one call that creates a node; calls with an empty range just return None):

CallRoot taken from preordermiddleLeft rangeRight range
build(0, 4)310..02..4
build(0, 0)900..-1 (empty)1..0 (empty)
build(2, 4)2032..24..4
build(2, 2)152emptyempty
build(4, 4)74emptyempty

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for the map (plus O(h) recursion).

Hard 124. Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum Binary Tree

Problem: A path is any chain of connected nodes (it doesn't have to pass through the root, and it can't branch). Return the largest possible sum of node values on a path. Values may be negative.

Spot it: "max path" in a tree, and the best answer at a node depends on the best answers below it. That's postorder.

Key insight: Each node does two different jobs. (1) It updates the global best with a path that bends at it: val + left + right. (2) It returns to its parent a path that goes down only one side: val + max(left, right). A parent can only extend one branch. Clamp negative branch gains to 0 (just don't take that branch).

Approach:

  1. Write a helper method gain(node) = the best sum of a path that starts at node and goes down one side.
  2. Postorder: compute left_gain and right_gain from the children, and replace a negative gain with 0. Negative branches are dropped.
  3. Update self.best with node.val + left_gain + right_gain, the path that bends at this node.
  4. Return node.val plus the bigger of left_gain and right_gain. A parent can extend only one branch.
  5. The answer is self.best after calling self.gain(root).
class Solution:
    def maxPathSum(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        # Best path sum seen anywhere so far. Start at "minus infinity"
        # so that even a single negative node can beat it.
        self.best = float("-inf")
        self.gain(root)           # walks the whole tree and updates self.best
        return self.best

    def gain(self, node: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        # Helper method: best sum of a path that STARTS at node and goes DOWN one side.
        if node is None:
            return 0
        # Postorder: get the children's answers first.
        left_gain = self.gain(node.left)
        if left_gain < 0:
            left_gain = 0         # a negative branch only hurts: don't take it
        right_gain = self.gain(node.right)
        if right_gain < 0:
            right_gain = 0
        # Job 1: a path that BENDS here uses both sides. Is it the best so far?
        path_through_node = node.val + left_gain + right_gain
        if path_through_node > self.best:
            self.best = path_through_node
        # Job 2: the parent can extend only ONE side, so return the better one.
        if left_gain > right_gain:
            return node.val + left_gain
        else:
            return node.val + right_gain

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. maxPathSum sets self.best to minus infinity, calls the helper gain on the root, and returns whatever best was found.
  2. gain(node) returns the best sum of a path that starts at node and goes down one side. An empty subtree gives 0.
  3. It first computes the children's gains (postorder). A negative gain is replaced by 0, meaning "don't go down that branch".
  4. path_through_node is a path that bends at this node and uses both sides. If it beats self.best, it becomes the new best.
  5. Finally it returns the node's value plus the better of the two sides, because a parent can only continue the path down one side.

Dry run on root = [-10,9,20,null,null,15,7] (rows are in postorder, the order gain finishes):

-10935344225

The answer is 42: the path 15 → 20 → 7.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space.

Hard 297. Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree Binary Tree

Problem: Design serialize(root) -> str and deserialize(str) -> root so that a tree survives the round trip.

Spot it: "encode/decode a tree": preorder with explicit null markers is self-describing.

Key insight: If you write # for every missing child, a preorder string alone determines the tree. That's different from 105, which needed two traversals. Deserialize by reading tokens in the same preorder: make the node, then build its left, then its right.

Approach:

  1. Serialize: preorder walk (helper method serialize_walk). Write the value for a node and # for every missing child, then join with commas.
  2. Deserialize: split on commas and keep self.position, the index of the next token to read.
  3. deserialize_build() reads one token. # means None. Otherwise create the node, then call deserialize_build() for its left, then its right.
  4. Because both directions use the same preorder, the tokens are consumed in exactly the order they were written.
class Codec:
    def serialize(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> str:
        tokens = []                       # one string per node, "#" for a missing child
        self.serialize_walk(root, tokens)
        # [1,2,3,null,null,4,5] -> "1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,#"
        return ",".join(tokens)

    def serialize_walk(self, node: Optional[TreeNode], tokens: List[str]) -> None:
        # Helper method: PREORDER walk (me, then left, then right).
        if node is None:
            tokens.append("#")            # null marker keeps the shape of the tree
            return
        tokens.append(str(node.val))
        self.serialize_walk(node.left, tokens)
        self.serialize_walk(node.right, tokens)

    def deserialize(self, data: str) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        self.tokens = data.split(",")     # "1,2,#" -> ["1", "2", "#"]
        self.position = 0                 # index of the next token to read
        return self.deserialize_build()

    def deserialize_build(self) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        # Helper method: read tokens in the SAME preorder that serialize wrote them.
        token = self.tokens[self.position]
        self.position = self.position + 1
        if token == "#":
            return None                   # a missing child
        node = TreeNode(int(token))
        node.left = self.deserialize_build()     # next tokens describe the left subtree
        node.right = self.deserialize_build()    # then the right subtree
        return node

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. serialize creates an empty list tokens, lets the helper method serialize_walk fill it, and joins the tokens with commas.
  2. serialize_walk is a preorder walk: a missing child adds "#"; a real node adds its value, then walks left, then right.
  3. deserialize splits the string back into a list and sets self.position = 0, the index of the next token to read.
  4. deserialize_build reads one token and moves the position on. "#" means None. Otherwise it creates the node and builds its left child, then its right child, from the following tokens.
  5. Because both directions use the same preorder (me, left, right), tokens are read back in exactly the order they were written.

Dry run of serialize on [1,2,3,null,null,4,5]:

StepVisitingtokens joined so far
1node 11
2node 21,2
32's left (None)1,2,#
42's right (None)1,2,#,#
5node 31,2,#,#,3
6node 41,2,#,#,3,4
74's left (None)1,2,#,#,3,4,#
84's right (None)1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#
9node 51,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5
105's left (None)1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#
115's right (None)1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,#

deserialize reads those 11 tokens in the same order: 1 becomes the root, 2 its left child, the two # close 2's children, 3 becomes the root's right child, and so on.

Complexity: O(n) time and space for both directions.

8. Common mistakes

Forgetting the base caseEvery recursive tree function must handle node is None first, or you'll get AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'left'.
Validating a BST by comparing only parent and childThe BST rule applies to the whole subtree. Use inorder + prev, or pass (lo, hi) bounds down.
Pushing left before right in iterative preorderA stack is last-in-first-out. Push right first so left pops first.
Not freezing len(queue) in level orderIf you loop while queue without capturing the size first, children of this level mix into the current level.
Re-computing subtree info (O(n²))Calling height() inside every node's check (as in "is balanced" or "diameter") re-walks subtrees. Return the height from the same postorder pass.
Deep trees and recursion limitsPython's default recursion limit is about 1000. A 105-node "stick" tree will crash a recursive solution. Use the iterative versions, or sys.setrecursionlimit when the tree is guaranteed balanced.

9. Self-check quiz

You need the diameter of a tree, which requires each node to know the heights of both of its subtrees. Which order?

The node needs answers from its children before it can compute its own, so information flows up. That's postorder.

Inorder traversal of the BST [4,2,6,1,3,5,7] gives…

Inorder of a BST is always sorted. The other two are preorder and postorder of the same tree.

"Return the values you'd see standing on the right side of the tree, top to bottom."

"Top to bottom, one per row" is a per-level question. Do level order and take the last node of each level. (A preorder DFS that visits right first and records the first node at each new depth also works.)

Extra space used by a recursive DFS on a tree of height h?

The call stack holds one frame per ancestor of the current node, so at most h frames. That's log n when balanced and n when it's a stick.

Easy 94. Binary Tree Inorder Traversal Binary TreeStack

Problem: Return the values of a binary tree in inorder (left, node, right). Do it without recursion.

Spot it: "inorder" is literally in the name. The iterative version is the building block for 98, 173 and 230.

Approach:

  1. Keep a stack of ancestors you still need to come back to, and a pointer current.
  2. Slide down-left from current, pushing every node.
  3. Pop: that's the leftmost node not yet visited. Record its value.
  4. Move to its right child and repeat until both current is None and the stack is empty.
class Solution:
    def inorderTraversal(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[int]:
        out = []                  # the answer, in inorder
        stack = []                # ancestors we still have to come back to
        current = root
        # Still a node to visit, or an ancestor to return to?
        while current is not None or len(stack) > 0:
            # Slide left, remembering every ancestor.
            while current is not None:
                stack.append(current)
                current = current.left
            # Leftmost node not visited yet.
            current = stack.pop()
            out.append(current.val)   # INORDER: record between left and right
            # Now handle its right subtree.
            current = current.right
        return out

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. out is the answer, stack holds ancestors still to be visited, current is our position.
  2. The inner while slides left from current, pushing each node.
  3. stack.pop() returns the leftmost node not yet visited. Its value is recorded (left side is already done, right side comes next: that's inorder).
  4. current = current.right moves into the right subtree. The outer loop stops when there is no current node and the stack is empty.

Dry run on root = [1,null,2,3] (1 at the root, 2 its right child, 3 the left child of 2):

StepStack after sliding leftPoppedout so far
1[1]1[1]
2[2, 3]3[1, 3]
3[2]2[1, 3, 2]

Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space.

Medium 102. Binary Tree Level Order Traversal Binary TreeQueue

Problem: Return the node values level by level, from top to bottom and left to right within each level, as a list of lists.

Spot it: "level by level" means BFS on the tree with a queue.

Approach:

  1. If the tree is empty, return []. Otherwise put the root in a deque.
  2. While the queue isn't empty, freeze level_size = len(queue).
  3. Pop exactly level_size nodes, collect their values into level, and push their children.
  4. Append level to the result.
class Solution:
    def levelOrder(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[List[int]]:
        if root is None:
            return []
        result = []
        # deque: queue.append(x) adds at the BACK, queue.popleft() takes from the FRONT.
        queue = deque()
        queue.append(root)
        while len(queue) > 0:
            level_size = len(queue)       # freeze: exactly the nodes of THIS level
            level = []
            for _ in range(level_size):
                node = queue.popleft()
                level.append(node.val)
                # Children go to the back of the queue: they are the next level.
                if node.left is not None:
                    queue.append(node.left)
                if node.right is not None:
                    queue.append(node.right)
            result.append(level)
        return result

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. An empty tree returns []. Otherwise the root goes into the queue.
  2. Each round of the outer loop handles one level. level_size is read first, so later children don't sneak into this level.
  3. The inner loop pops exactly level_size nodes from the front, records their values, and appends their children to the back.
  4. The finished level list is appended to result.

Dry run on root = [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]:

RoundQueue at startlevel_sizelevelQueue after
1[3]1[3][9, 20]
2[9, 20]2[9, 20][15, 7]
3[15, 7]2[15, 7][]

Result: [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]].

Complexity: O(n) time, O(w) space (w = widest level).

Medium 103. Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal Binary TreeQueue

Problem: Like level order, but alternate direction: level 0 left→right, level 1 right→left, and so on.

Spot it: Still "per level", so it's level order. Only the way each level is written changes.

Approach:

  1. Run the normal level-order BFS. The queue order stays left→right.
  2. For each level, collect values into a list level, always left to right.
  3. When going left→right add level as it is. When going right→left copy it backwards (with a while loop) and add the copy.
  4. Flip the direction flag after every level.
class Solution:
    def zigzagLevelOrder(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[List[int]]:
        if root is None:
            return []
        result = []
        # deque: queue.append(x) adds at the BACK, queue.popleft() takes from the FRONT.
        queue = deque()
        queue.append(root)
        left_to_right = True              # direction for the current level
        while len(queue) > 0:
            level_size = len(queue)       # freeze the size of this level
            level = []                    # values of this level, always left to right
            for _ in range(level_size):
                node = queue.popleft()
                level.append(node.val)
                # Children ALWAYS go in left-to-right; only the output is flipped.
                if node.left is not None:
                    queue.append(node.left)
                if node.right is not None:
                    queue.append(node.right)
            if left_to_right:
                result.append(level)
            else:
                # Copy the level backwards into a new list.
                reversed_level = []
                i = len(level) - 1
                while i >= 0:
                    reversed_level.append(level[i])
                    i = i - 1
                result.append(reversed_level)
            left_to_right = not left_to_right     # flip the direction for the next level
        return result

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. This is the level-order code from 102, plus a flag left_to_right that starts as True.
  2. Inside each level the queue is handled exactly as in 102, so level is always collected left to right.
  3. If the flag is True, level is added as it is. If it is False, a while loop copies it from the last item to the first into reversed_level, and that is added instead.
  4. left_to_right = not left_to_right flips the direction after every level.

Dry run on root = [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]:

RoundQueue at startlevel (left to right)left_to_rightAdded to result
1[3][3]True[3]
2[9, 20][9, 20]False[20, 9]
3[15, 7][15, 7]True[15, 7]

Result: [[3], [20, 9], [15, 7]].

Complexity: O(n) time, O(w) space.

Medium 199. Binary Tree Right Side View Binary TreeQueue

Problem: Imagine standing to the right of the tree. Return the values you can see, from top to bottom. That's the rightmost node of each level.

Spot it: "one value per row, top to bottom" is a per-level question, so level order.

Approach:

  1. Run level-order BFS with a frozen size.
  2. While popping the level_size nodes of a level, remember the last one popped.
  3. After the level ends, append that last value: it's the rightmost node.
class Solution:
    def rightSideView(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[int]:
        if root is None:
            return []
        view = []                         # one value per level: the rightmost one
        # deque: queue.append(x) adds at the BACK, queue.popleft() takes from the FRONT.
        queue = deque()
        queue.append(root)
        while len(queue) > 0:
            level_size = len(queue)       # freeze the size of this level
            for i in range(level_size):
                node = queue.popleft()
                # The last node popped in this level is the rightmost one.
                if i == level_size - 1:
                    view.append(node.val)
                if node.left is not None:
                    queue.append(node.left)
                if node.right is not None:
                    queue.append(node.right)
        return view

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. An empty tree has no view. Otherwise start the queue with the root.
  2. Each round freezes level_size and pops exactly that many nodes, so one round = one level.
  3. The counter i tells us how many nodes of this level we have popped. When i == level_size - 1 it's the last one, which is the rightmost node, so its value goes into view.
  4. Children are pushed left then right, keeping the queue in left-to-right order for the next level.

Dry run on root = [1,2,3,null,5,null,4]:

RoundQueue at startlevel_sizeLast node poppedview so far
1[1]11[1]
2[2, 3]23[1, 3]
3[5, 4]24[1, 3, 4]

Complexity: O(n) time, O(w) space.

Medium 236. Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree Binary Tree

Problem: Given two nodes p and q in a binary tree (not a BST), return their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both of them in its subtree. A node counts as its own descendant.

Spot it: Each node needs to know "did my left / right subtree contain p or q?". That information flows up, so postorder.

Approach:

  1. Base case: if the node is None, return None; if it is p or q, return it as is.
  2. Recurse into the left and right subtrees.
  3. If both sides returned something non-null, p and q are split across this node, so this node is the LCA.
  4. Otherwise return whichever side is non-null. It carries p, q, or the LCA found deeper down.
class Solution:
    # LeetCode calls the two targets p and q; here they are named node_p and node_q.
    def lowestCommonAncestor(self, root: 'TreeNode', node_p: 'TreeNode', node_q: 'TreeNode') -> 'TreeNode':
        # Ran off the tree: nothing found down here.
        if root is None:
            return None
        # Found one of the targets: report it to the parent.
        if root is node_p or root is node_q:
            return root
        # Postorder: ask both subtrees first.
        found_left = self.lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, node_p, node_q)
        found_right = self.lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, node_p, node_q)
        # One target on each side: this node is where they split, so it is the LCA.
        if found_left is not None and found_right is not None:
            return root
        # Otherwise pass up whatever was found (it may be None).
        if found_left is not None:
            return found_left
        return found_right

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. LeetCode names the two target nodes p and q. The code calls them node_p and node_q so the names say what they are; LeetCode passes them by position, so this still works there.
  2. If root is None we fell off the tree: nothing found, return None.
  3. If root is node_p or node_q, return it. We don't need to look below it: if the other target is underneath, this node is the LCA anyway.
  4. Otherwise search both subtrees (postorder) and keep what each one reports in found_left and found_right.
  5. If both are non-None, one target is on each side, so this node is the lowest common ancestor.
  6. Otherwise pass up whichever side found something (or None if neither did).

Dry run on root = [3,5,1,6,2,0,8,null,null,7,4], p = 5, q = 1:

Call on nodeWhat happensReturns
5it is p, stop here (6, 2, 7, 4 are never visited)node 5
1it is q, stop herenode 1
3found_left = 5, found_right = 1, both non-Nonenode 3

Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space.

Medium 173. Binary Search Tree Iterator BSTStack

Problem: Design an iterator over a BST: next() returns the next smallest value, and hasNext() says whether any remain. Aim for average O(1) time and O(h) memory.

Spot it: "next smallest" in a BST is inorder. To "pause" between calls, keep the iterative inorder stack as object state.

Approach:

  1. In the constructor, push the root and all of its left descendants (the "slide left" step).
  2. next(): pop the top node. That's the answer.
  3. Before returning, slide left from that node's right child, pushing nodes. That prepares the next call.
  4. hasNext() is just "is the stack non-empty?".
class BSTIterator:
    def __init__(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]):
        self.stack = []                   # the paused iterative-inorder stack
        self.push_left(root)              # smallest value ends up on top

    def push_left(self, node: Optional[TreeNode]) -> None:
        # The "slide left" step of iterative inorder: push node and all its left descendants.
        while node is not None:
            self.stack.append(node)
            node = node.left

    def next(self) -> int:
        node = self.stack.pop()           # next smallest value
        self.push_left(node.right)        # its successor lives in the right subtree
        return node.val

    def hasNext(self) -> bool:
        # Values remain exactly when the stack is not empty.
        return len(self.stack) > 0

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The constructor creates an empty stack and calls push_left(root), so the path down to the smallest value is on the stack with the smallest on top.
  2. push_left(node) is the "slide left" step of iterative inorder: push the node, move to its left child, repeat until None.
  3. next() pops the top node (the next smallest value). Before returning, it slides left from that node's right child, so the following value is ready on top.
  4. hasNext() returns True while the stack still holds nodes.
  5. Each node is pushed once and popped once, so over all calls next() costs O(1) on average.

Dry run on root = [7,3,15,null,null,9,20]:

CallReturnsStack afterwards (top is last)
BSTIterator(root)-[7, 3]
next()3[7]
next()7[15, 9]
next()9[15]
next()15[20]
next()20[]
hasNext()False[]

Complexity: next() is amortized O(1) because each node is pushed and popped once. O(h) memory.

Easy 100. Same Tree Binary Tree

Problem: Return True if the two binary trees p and q have the same shape and the same values.

Spot it: Compare two trees node by node → one recursion that takes a node from each tree.

Approach:

  1. Both nodes missing → equal so far: True.
  2. Exactly one missing, or the values differ → False.
  3. Otherwise both left subtrees must be the same and both right subtrees must be the same.
class Solution:
    def isSameTree(self, p: Optional[TreeNode], q: Optional[TreeNode]) -> bool:
        if p is None and q is None:
            return True            # both empty: identical
        if p is None or q is None:
            return False           # only one is empty: different shape
        if p.val != q.val:
            return False           # same position, different value
        # identical only if BOTH pairs of subtrees are identical
        return self.isSameTree(p.left, q.left) and self.isSameTree(p.right, q.right)

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. if p is None and q is None: return True: two empty trees match.
  2. if p is None or q is None: return False: we already know they aren't both None, so exactly one is. The shapes differ.
  3. if p.val != q.val: return False: same position, different value.
  4. return ... and ...: both subtrees must match. and stops early: if the left side fails, the right side is never checked.

Dry run on the example:

p = [1, 2], q = [1, null, 2] (LeetCode Example 2). Returns False.

compare (p node, q node)resultwhy
(1, 1)check childrenboth exist, values equal
(2, None) (the left children)Falseonly one exists
(1, 1)Falseand short-circuits: the right children are never compared

Complexity: O(min(m, n)) time (stops at the first difference), O(h) recursion space.

Easy 101. Symmetric Tree Binary Tree

Problem: Return True if the tree is a mirror image of itself around its centre.

Spot it: A tree is symmetric when its left subtree mirrors its right subtree. "Mirror" is Same Tree with crossed children: a.left pairs with b.right, and a.right with b.left.

Approach:

  1. Write a helper mirror(a, b) that checks whether two subtrees mirror each other.
  2. Both missing → True; one missing or values differ → False.
  3. Otherwise the outer pair (a.left, b.right) and the inner pair (a.right, b.left) must both mirror.
  4. The answer is mirror(root.left, root.right).
class Solution:
    def isSymmetric(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> bool:
        def mirror(a, b):
            if a is None and b is None:
                return True
            if a is None or b is None:
                return False
            if a.val != b.val:
                return False
            # outer children pair up, and inner children pair up
            return mirror(a.left, b.right) and mirror(a.right, b.left)

        return mirror(root.left, root.right)

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. def mirror(a, b): true when the subtree at a is the mirror image of the subtree at b.
  2. The first three checks are the same as Same Tree: matching emptiness and equal values.
  3. mirror(a.left, b.right): the outer edges of the two halves must match.
  4. mirror(a.right, b.left): and so must the inner ones.
  5. return mirror(root.left, root.right): the root itself sits on the mirror line, so only its two subtrees are compared.

Dry run on the example:

root = [1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 3] (LeetCode Example 1). Returns True. Call the two 2s 2L and 2R.

mirror(a, b)valuesnext checksresult
(2L, 2R)2 = 2outer (3, 3), inner (4, 4)waits
(3, 3)3 = 3both pairs of children are (None, None)True
(4, 4)4 = 4both pairs of children are (None, None)True
(2L, 2R)True and TrueTrue

Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) recursion space.

Easy 104. Maximum Depth of Binary Tree Binary Tree

Problem: Return the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.

Spot it: A value that depends on both subtrees → post-order recursion: ask each child for its depth, then combine.

Approach:

  1. An empty tree has depth 0.
  2. Get the depth of the left and right subtrees recursively.
  3. This node adds one level: return 1 + max(left, right).
class Solution:
    def maxDepth(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        if root is None:
            return 0
        left_depth = self.maxDepth(root.left)
        right_depth = self.maxDepth(root.right)
        # this node is one more level on top of its deeper subtree
        return 1 + max(left_depth, right_depth)

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. if root is None: return 0: no node, no depth. This is what makes a leaf's depth come out as 1.
  2. left_depth, right_depth: the recursion answers the same question for each subtree.
  3. return 1 + max(...): the longest path goes through the deeper side, plus this node.

Easy 108. Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree BSTArray

Problem: nums is sorted ascending. Build a height-balanced BST from it (subtree heights differ by at most 1 at every node).

Spot it: BST + sorted input: the in-order of the tree must equal nums. Picking the middle element as the root puts half of the values on each side, which keeps the tree balanced. Then do the same for each half.

Approach:

  1. build(lo, hi) builds a tree from nums[lo..hi]; an empty range gives None.
  2. mid = (lo + hi) // 2 becomes the root.
  3. The left subtree is build(lo, mid − 1), the right is build(mid + 1, hi).
  4. Return build(0, n − 1).
class Solution:
    def sortedArrayToBST(self, nums: List[int]) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        def build(lo, hi):
            if lo > hi:
                return None              # empty range: no node
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            node = TreeNode(nums[mid])
            # smaller values on the left, larger on the right
            node.left = build(lo, mid - 1)
            node.right = build(mid + 1, hi)
            return node

        return build(0, len(nums) - 1)

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. def build(lo, hi): works on index ranges instead of slicing, so no list copies are made.
  2. if lo > hi: return None: an empty range is a missing child.
  3. mid = (lo + hi) // 2, TreeNode(nums[mid]): the middle value; the two halves differ in size by at most 1, which is what keeps the tree balanced.
  4. node.left = build(lo, mid - 1): everything smaller; node.right = build(mid + 1, hi): everything larger. That's exactly the BST rule.

(4, 4)49NoneNone

Complexity: O(n) time (each element becomes one node), O(log n) recursion depth.

Easy 110. Balanced Binary Tree Binary Tree

Problem: A tree is height-balanced if, at every node, the heights of its two subtrees differ by at most 1. Check it.

Spot it: Each node needs both subtree heights → post-order. Computing heights separately at every node costs O(n²); instead return the height and use -1 to mean "already unbalanced below".

Approach:

  1. A helper height(node) returns the subtree's height, or -1 if it is unbalanced anywhere.
  2. Empty tree → height 0.
  3. Get both child heights; if either is -1, pass the -1 up immediately.
  4. If they differ by more than 1, return -1. Otherwise return 1 + max(left, right).
  5. The tree is balanced if height(root) != -1.
class Solution:
    def isBalanced(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> bool:
        def height(node):
            # returns the height, or -1 if this subtree is unbalanced somewhere
            if node is None:
                return 0
            left = height(node.left)
            if left == -1:
                return -1
            right = height(node.right)
            if right == -1:
                return -1
            if abs(left - right) > 1:
                return -1
            return 1 + max(left, right)

        return height(root) != -1

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. def height(node): one function, two jobs: the height, and an "unbalanced" flag (-1, which can never be a real height).
  2. if node is None: return 0: empty subtrees have height 0.
  3. if left == -1: return -1: an unbalanced subtree makes the whole tree unbalanced. Stop early (we don't even visit the right side).
  4. if abs(left - right) > 1: return -1: this node itself breaks the rule.
  5. return 1 + max(left, right): the normal height.
  6. return height(root) != -1: balanced exactly when no -1 reached the top.

height(root) is −1, so isBalanced returns False. The root is the only node that breaks the rule.

Complexity: O(n) time (each node visited once), O(h) recursion space.

Easy 226. Invert Binary Tree Binary Tree

Problem: Mirror the binary tree (swap every node's left and right children) and return its root.

Spot it: "Do something to every node" on a tree → a recursive traversal. Each node's job is local: swap its two children.

Approach:

  1. An empty tree is already inverted: return None.
  2. Recursively invert the left subtree and the right subtree.
  3. Swap them: the inverted right becomes the new left and vice versa.
  4. Return the node.
class Solution:
    def invertTree(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        if root is None:
            return None
        # invert both subtrees first (post-order) ...
        left = self.invertTree(root.left)
        right = self.invertTree(root.right)
        # ... then swap them
        root.left = right
        root.right = left
        return root

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. if root is None: return None: the base case. Every leaf's missing children end here.
  2. left = self.invertTree(root.left) and right = ...: trust the recursion to mirror each subtree completely.
  3. root.left = right, root.right = left: swap the two (already mirrored) subtrees. Saving them in variables first means no temporary is needed.
  4. return root: the parent call attaches this mirrored subtree on its opposite side.

Dry run on the example:

call finisheschildren after the swap (left, right)

2(3, 1)
6(None, None)

7(9, 6)

Complexity: O(n) time (every node once), O(h) space for the recursion stack (h = height).

Easy 530. Minimum Absolute Difference in BST BST

Problem: Return the minimum absolute difference between the values of any two different nodes in a BST.

Spot it: An in-order traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order, and in a sorted list the closest pair is always adjacent. So walk in order and compare each value with the previous one.

Approach:

  1. Do an in-order traversal (left, node, right), remembering the previously visited value prev.
  2. At each node, if there is a prev, update best with node.val − prev.
  3. Set prev = node.val and continue to the right subtree.
class Solution:
    def getMinimumDifference(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        prev = None             # value of the previous node in sorted order
        best = float("inf")

        def inorder(node):
            nonlocal prev, best
            if node is None:
                return
            inorder(node.left)
            if prev is not None:
                # sorted order: the closest value to node.val is its neighbour
                best = min(best, node.val - prev)
            prev = node.val
            inorder(node.right)

        inorder(root)
        return best

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. prev = None: no value visited yet. best = float("inf"): any real difference beats infinity.
  2. inorder(node.left) → handle node → inorder(node.right): that order lists BST values from smallest to largest.
  3. if prev is not None: best = min(best, node.val - prev): values are increasing, so the difference is never negative and abs isn't needed.
  4. prev = node.val: this node becomes the neighbour of the next one.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) recursion space.

Easy 543. Diameter of Binary Tree Binary Tree

Problem: The diameter is the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes. The path does not have to pass through the root. Return it.

Spot it: The longest path bends at some node: down its left side and down its right side. At every node, left height + right height is a candidate. Post-order recursion gives both heights; a variable outside the recursion keeps the best candidate.

Approach:

  1. best = 0 holds the longest path seen.
  2. A helper height(node) returns how many nodes are on the longest downward path from node (0 for None).
  3. At each node: get the left and right heights. The path that bends here has left + right edges; update best.
  4. Return 1 + max(left, right) to the parent.
class Solution:
    def diameterOfBinaryTree(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        best = 0

        def height(node):
            nonlocal best
            if node is None:
                return 0
            left = height(node.left)
            right = height(node.right)
            # the longest path that bends at this node uses left + right edges
            best = max(best, left + right)
            # the parent can only extend ONE side of this node
            return 1 + max(left, right)

        height(root)
        return best

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. best = 0: the answer, updated as the recursion visits every node.
  2. nonlocal best: lets the inner function change best from the outer function (without it, Python would create a new local best).
  3. left = height(node.left), right = height(node.right): nodes on the longest path down each side.
  4. best = max(best, left + right): going down left nodes on one side and right nodes on the other is a path of exactly left + right edges through this node.
  5. return 1 + max(left, right): a parent can continue the path through only one of our sides, so it gets the taller one.

Dry run on the example:

Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) recursion space.

Easy 572. Subtree of Another Tree Binary Tree

Problem: Return True if some node of root, together with all its descendants, is identical to the tree subRoot.

Spot it: Two layers: a traversal that visits every candidate node of root, and Same Tree (LeetCode 100) to compare a candidate with subRoot.

Approach:

  1. Write same(a, b) exactly as in Same Tree.
  2. If root is None, there is nothing to match: False.
  3. If same(root, subRoot), we're done: True.
  4. Otherwise the match must be inside the left or right subtree: recurse.
class Solution:
    def isSubtree(self, root: Optional[TreeNode], subRoot: Optional[TreeNode]) -> bool:
        def same(a, b):
            if a is None and b is None:
                return True
            if a is None or b is None or a.val != b.val:
                return False
            return same(a.left, b.left) and same(a.right, b.right)

        if root is None:
            return False
        if same(root, subRoot):
            return True
        # not at this node: try every node below it
        return self.isSubtree(root.left, subRoot) or self.isSubtree(root.right, subRoot)

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. def same(a, b): LeetCode 100 in a few lines: equal shape and equal values.
  2. if root is None: return False: ran out of candidates on this path.
  3. if same(root, subRoot): return True: the subtree starting here matches exactly.
  4. return ... or ...: look for a match anywhere in the left subtree, otherwise anywhere in the right subtree. or stops at the first success.

Dry run on the example:

3no3 ≠ 4
4yes4 = 4, then (1, 1) and (2, 2) match, all leaves end together

The left subtree of 3 matched, so or never needs to try the 5.

Complexity: O(m · n) time in the worst case (Same Tree from each of the m nodes), O(h) recursion space.

Medium 106. Construct Binary Tree from Inorder and Postorder Traversal Binary TreeHash Map

Problem: Given the in-order and post-order traversals of a binary tree with unique values, rebuild the tree.

Spot it: Mirror of LeetCode 105. Post-order is left, right, root, so the root is at the end. Its position in the in-order list splits the values into the left subtree and the right subtree.

Key insight: Reading post-order backwards gives root, right, left. So take values from the end of postorder and build the right subtree before the left one. A dictionary value → in-order index makes each split O(1).

Approach:

  1. Map every value to its index in inorder.
  2. Keep a pointer post_i at the last element of postorder.
  3. build(lo, hi) builds the subtree whose values are inorder[lo..hi]: take postorder[post_i] as the root and move post_i left.
  4. Find the root's in-order index mid. Build the right subtree from mid + 1..hi first, then the left from lo..mid − 1.
  5. An empty range returns None.
class Solution:
    def buildTree(self, inorder: List[int], postorder: List[int]) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        # value -> its position in inorder, to split left/right in O(1)
        index_of = {}
        for i in range(len(inorder)):
            index_of[inorder[i]] = i
        # we consume postorder from the END: root, then right subtree, then left
        post_i = len(postorder) - 1

        def build(lo, hi):
            nonlocal post_i
            if lo > hi:
                return None
            root_val = postorder[post_i]
            post_i = post_i - 1
            node = TreeNode(root_val)
            mid = index_of[root_val]
            # right first, because postorder read backwards is root, right, left
            node.right = build(mid + 1, hi)
            node.left = build(lo, mid - 1)
            return node

        return build(0, len(inorder) - 1)

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. index_of: where each value sits in inorder. Values are unique, so this is well defined.
  2. post_i = len(postorder) - 1: the next root to use, starting from the end.
  3. if lo > hi: return None: no values for this subtree.
  4. root_val = postorder[post_i], post_i = post_i - 1: take the next root.
  5. mid = index_of[root_val]: in-order values left of mid form the left subtree and values right of it form the right subtree.
  6. node.right = build(mid + 1, hi) before node.left: the element just before a root in post-order belongs to its right subtree. Building left first would hand the left subtree the wrong roots.

(0, 0)90emptyempty

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for the map and recursion.

Medium 114. Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List Binary TreeLinked List

Problem: Flatten the tree in place into a "linked list" that uses the right pointers, in pre-order (node, left, right). Every left pointer must become None.

Spot it: Pre-order puts the whole left subtree between a node and its right subtree. So for each node with a left child: hang the right subtree off the rightmost node of the left subtree, then move the left subtree over to the right. O(1) extra space, no recursion.

Approach:

  1. Walk cur down the right pointers from the root.
  2. If cur has a left subtree: find that subtree's rightmost node tail (the last node of the left subtree in pre-order).
  3. Attach cur.right to tail.right, then make cur.right = cur.left and cur.left = None.
  4. Move cur = cur.right and repeat until cur is None.
class Solution:
    def flatten(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> None:
        cur = root
        while cur is not None:
            if cur.left is not None:
                # the last node of the left subtree in pre-order is its rightmost node
                tail = cur.left
                while tail.right is not None:
                    tail = tail.right
                # the right subtree comes after the whole left subtree
                tail.right = cur.right
                # move the left subtree into the right slot
                cur.right = cur.left
                cur.left = None
            cur = cur.right

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. cur = root: we work down the chain that is being built.
  2. if cur.left is not None: only nodes with a left subtree need re-wiring.
  3. tail = cur.left, then while tail.right is not None: tail = tail.right: the rightmost node of the left subtree is visited last in pre-order, so the right subtree must follow it.
  4. tail.right = cur.right: hang the old right subtree after that last node.
  5. cur.right = cur.left, cur.left = None: the left subtree now comes right after cur, and no left pointers remain.
  6. cur = cur.right: continue. Nodes deeper down still get the same treatment when cur reaches them.

Complexity: O(n) time (each tail walk covers edges no other walk covers), O(1) extra space.

Medium 235. Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree BST

Problem: In a BST, return the lowest node that has both p and q as descendants (a node counts as a descendant of itself).

Spot it: BST order tells you which side each value is on. While both values are smaller than the current node, the LCA is on the left; while both are larger, on the right. The first node where they split (or that equals one of them) is the LCA.

Approach:

  1. Start at the root.
  2. If both p.val and q.val are smaller than node.val, move left.
  3. If both are larger, move right.
  4. Otherwise they are on different sides (or one of them is this node): return it.
class Solution:
    def lowestCommonAncestor(self, root: TreeNode, p: TreeNode, q: TreeNode) -> TreeNode:
        node = root
        while node is not None:
            if p.val < node.val and q.val < node.val:
                node = node.left      # both are in the left subtree
            elif p.val > node.val and q.val > node.val:
                node = node.right     # both are in the right subtree
            else:
                # they split here (or one of them IS this node)
                return node
        return None

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. node = root: an iterative walk. No recursion is needed because we only ever go down one path.
  2. if p.val < node.val and q.val < node.val: in a BST everything smaller lives on the left, so the LCA must be there too.
  3. elif p.val > node.val and q.val > node.val: both on the right.
  4. else: return node: one value is ≤ and the other ≥ this node, so this is the deepest node above both.
  5. return None: unreachable when p and q are in the tree, as the problem guarantees.

Dry run on the example:

nodep = 2 vs nodeq = 4 vs nodemove
6smallersmallergo left
2equallargersplit → return 2

Complexity: O(h) time (one root-to-node path), O(1) space.

Medium 427. Construct Quad Tree MatrixQuad Tree

Problem: grid is an n × n matrix of 0s and 1s (n a power of 2). Build its quad tree: a uniform square becomes a leaf with that value; otherwise the node has four children for the top-left, top-right, bottom-left and bottom-right quarters.

Spot it: A tree defined by recursive splitting → recursion that builds one node per square. Each node has four children instead of two.

Approach:

  1. build(row, col, size) handles the square whose top-left corner is (row, col).
  2. Check whether every cell in it equals the first cell.
  3. If so, return a leaf: Node(val = that value, isLeaf = True).
  4. Otherwise split into four squares of size // 2 and return an internal node with those four children.
class Solution:
    def construct(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> "Node":
        def build(row, col, size):
            # is every cell in this square the same as its first cell?
            first = grid[row][col]
            uniform = True
            for r in range(row, row + size):
                for c in range(col, col + size):
                    if grid[r][c] != first:
                        uniform = False
                        break
                if not uniform:
                    break
            if uniform:
                return Node(first == 1, True)
            half = size // 2
            # not uniform: split into four quarters
            return Node(True, False,
                        build(row, col, half),                 # top-left
                        build(row, col + half, half),          # top-right
                        build(row + half, col, half),          # bottom-left
                        build(row + half, col + half, half))   # bottom-right

        return build(0, 0, len(grid))

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. def build(row, col, size): a square is described by its corner and side length, so no sub-grids are copied.
  2. The two nested loops compare every cell with first and break out at the first mismatch.
  3. if uniform: return Node(first == 1, True): a leaf. LeetCode stores the value as a boolean, so first == 1 turns 1/0 into True/False.
  4. half = size // 2: the side of each quarter.
  5. Node(True, False, ...): an internal node (isLeaf = False; its val can be anything) with four recursively built children, in the order top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right.

Dry run on the example:

grid = [[0, 1], [1, 0]] (LeetCode Example 1). Returns [[0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1], [1, 1], [1, 0]] (each pair is [isLeaf, val]).

build(row, col, size)cellsuniform?result

(0, 0, 1)0yesleaf val = False
(0, 1, 1)1yesleaf val = True
(1, 0, 1)1yesleaf val = True
(1, 1, 1)0yesleaf val = False

Complexity: O(n² log n) time (each level of splitting re-scans all cells once), O(log n) recursion depth.
